lessonTitle: Airway Management: Maintenance, Intubation and Rescue

blocks.text: A 58-year-old man is wheeled into recovery after a four-hour spinal operation. He is unrousable to voice, snoring loudly, and his chest and abdomen move out of phase with each other. Within seconds his saturation starts to drift down. Almost everything in airway management is about reading this picture and acting in the right order.

blocks.markdown: **Why the airway fails.** In an unconscious or anaesthetised patient, tone in the genioglossus and the pharyngeal muscles falls. The tongue and soft palate fall back against the posterior pharyngeal wall and the epiglottis can fold over the laryngeal inlet. This is the commonest cause of airway obstruction in an unconscious patient, and it is fixable in seconds with the right manoeuvre. Other causes include secretions, blood, foreign bodies, laryngospasm and swelling. Obstruction shows itself as noisy breathing (snoring, gurgling, stridor), paradoxical 'see-saw' chest and abdominal movement, accessory muscle use, an absent or flattened capnography waveform, and finally desaturation and cyanosis. Silence in a struggling patient is the most dangerous sign of all: complete obstruction moves no air and makes no sound.

blocks.title: Airway management
blocks.text: The set of skills and equipment used to keep a patient's route for gas exchange open (patent), protected from soiling, and connected to a source of oxygen. It runs from simple manoeuvres, through airway adjuncts and supraglottic airway devices, to tracheal intubation and, as a last resort, front-of-neck access.

blocks.markdown: **Simple manoeuvres and adjuncts (objective 1).** Start with the least invasive step and escalate. (1) *Head tilt and chin lift* extends the atlanto-occipital joint and lifts the tongue off the pharynx; avoid it where cervical spine injury is suspected. (2) *Jaw thrust*: the fingers sit behind the angles of the mandible and push the jaw forward, which moves the tongue and epiglottis anteriorly; it is the preferred technique with suspected cervical spine injury. (3) Give high-flow oxygen with a facemask and reservoir bag, and use a two-handed facemask hold with an assistant squeezing the bag if ventilation is needed. (4) Add an *airway adjunct* if the manoeuvres are not enough. An oropharyngeal airway (OPA, Guedel) is a curved plastic tube that holds the tongue forward; it is only tolerated by a deeply unconscious patient with no gag reflex, otherwise it provokes gagging, vomiting or laryngospasm. A nasopharyngeal airway (NPA) is a soft lubricated tube passed along the floor of the nose; it is tolerated by patients with an intact gag reflex but is used with caution in suspected base-of-skull fracture and in coagulopathy because of the risk of epistaxis.

Incisors (lips) to the angle of the mandible
No: use only in deep unconsciousness
Gagging, vomiting, laryngospasm; wrong size can push the tongue back or obstruct the larynx
Nasopharyngeal airway
Manufacturer's size guidance; a size that passes easily along the nasal floor
Yes, usually tolerated
Epistaxis; caution with base-of-skull fracture or coagulopathy; check the nostril is patent

Manufacturer weight-based size
No: needs deep anaesthesia or unconsciousness
Does not fully protect against aspiration; can leak at high pressures

blocks.title: Stepwise rescue of a snoring, unrousable patient
blocks.prompt: A 71-year-old woman is drowsy after a sedative premedication, has a GCS of 7, and is snoring with see-saw respiration and SpO2 89% on room air. Describe the sequence of actions.

steps.text: Call for help and say clearly that the airway is obstructed; at the same time start high-flow oxygen through a reservoir mask so that every later step buys time.

Open the airway with head tilt and chin lift (or jaw thrust if the cervical spine may be injured). Re-check by looking, listening and feeling for breathing for up to 10 seconds; confirm a capnography trace if monitored.

If obstruction persists and the patient does not gag, measure an OPA from the incisors to the angle of the mandible, insert it, and re-assess; if the patient gags, remove it and use a lubricated NPA instead.

If still obstructed, ventilate with a two-person facemask technique using the OPA or NPA; if that fails, think of a supraglottic airway device and escalate to the anaesthetist, using the difficult airway plan.

blocks.answer: Simple manoeuvres first, oxygen throughout, then adjuncts matched to the gag reflex, then escalation; help is called at the start, not after the failure.

blocks.markdown: **Intubation and the difficult airway plan (objective 2).** Tracheal intubation places a cuffed tube through the vocal cords. It secures the airway, allows controlled ventilation, and reduces (but does not abolish) the risk of aspiration. Indications include inability to protect or maintain the airway, need for prolonged ventilation, anticipated airway swelling, and many general anaesthetics. The principles are *preparation, positioning, preoxygenation, visualisation, confirmation and a stated plan*. The view at laryngoscopy is graded by Cormack and Lehane: grade 1 full view of the glottis, grade 2 only the posterior part of the glottis or arytenoids, grade 3 the epiglottis only, grade 4 no glottic structures or epiglottis. Grades 3 and 4 predict difficult intubation. Simple bedside predictors of difficulty include reduced mouth opening, short thyromental distance, high Mallampati class, limited neck extension, prominent upper incisors, a receding jaw, and a history of previous difficulty; none is perfectly sensitive, so unanticipated difficulty is always possible.

items: Check the equipment: suction, working laryngoscope with alternative blades, tubes in two sizes, bougie, supraglottic airway device, front-of-neck access kit.
Apply monitoring including waveform capnography, with IV access established.
Position the patient in the 'sniffing' or ramped position and preoxygenate with a tight-fitting mask.
State the plan aloud (Plan A, B, C and D) and agree who will do what if intubation fails.
Confirm tube placement by a sustained waveform capnography trace; auscultation alone is unreliable.

blocks.caption: Gas available at atmospheric pressure from a cylinder, assuming ideal gas behaviour at constant temperature. V_c is the internal (water) volume in litres and P_gauge the gauge pressure in bar above atmospheric. Time in minutes = V_usable divided by the flow in L/min.

blocks.title: Planning oxygen supply for a transfer
blocks.prompt: A cylinder of internal volume 4.0 L reads 150 bar on its gauge. A patient needs 15 L/min through a reservoir mask. How long will the cylinder last, and how should the answer be used?

steps.text: Usable volume at atmospheric pressure is internal volume multiplied by gauge pressure.
Divide by the flow rate to obtain time.
In practice, plan to arrive with a safety margin well above zero (the cylinder is not usable to the last litre and journeys are delayed) and carry a second cylinder, following local policy.

blocks.answer: About 40 minutes in theory; plan for noticeably less and carry spare oxygen.

blocks.markdown: **The failed airway (objective 3).** Difficult airways are common; failed ones that end in harm are mostly failures of recognition and escalation. Difficult Airway Society (DAS) guidance for unanticipated difficult intubation in adults (check the current version) sets out four plans. The overriding aims are oxygenation, limited attempts, early help and an explicit change of plan when one fails.

rows: A
Facemask ventilation and tracheal intubation, with optimisation between attempts
Up to three attempts by the first operator (a fourth by a more experienced colleague); oxygenation is the priority
B
Maintain oxygenation with a supraglottic airway device (second-generation device preferred)
Failed insertion after limited attempts, or inadequate oxygenation or ventilation
C
Return to facemask ventilation; ensure full neuromuscular relaxation; decide to wake the patient or proceed
If facemask ventilation is inadequate the patient is in a 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' (CICO) situation
D
Emergency front-of-neck access (a scalpel-bougie-tube technique is the recommended approach)
Declare CICO, ensure paralysis, and perform without delay
blocks.caption: Summary of Plans A to D in unanticipated difficult intubation. Check the current DAS algorithm and local policy for detail.

blocks.title: Call for help early
blocks.text: Ask for help when difficulty is first recognised, not when the saturation is 70%. Call a senior anaesthetist, bring the difficult airway trolley, and tell the whole team that the airway is difficult. Fixation on repeated laryngoscopy is a classic failure: after the allowed attempts, change the technique, the device or the plan.

blocks.title: Order of thinking
blocks.text: Oxygenate first, intubate second. Maintain the airway with the simplest effective step, limit attempts, change something between attempts, call for help early, and move to front-of-neck access without hesitation when oxygenation fails.

points: Airway obstruction in unconscious patients is usually the tongue and soft palate falling back: head tilt chin lift or jaw thrust, then adjuncts matched to the gag reflex.
An OPA is sized from incisors to the angle of the mandible and needs an absent gag reflex; an NPA suits patients who gag but needs caution in base-of-skull fracture.
Intubation requires preparation, positioning, preoxygenation, a stated plan and waveform capnography to confirm placement.
DAS Plans A to D give an escalation ladder; limit attempts, call help early and perform front-of-neck access if CICO is declared. Check current guidance.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man in recovery is unrousable, snoring and has see-saw chest movement. There is no suspicion of neck injury and his SpO2 is falling. Which is the most appropriate immediate action after calling for help?

options.text: Administer a sedative to settle the breathing pattern
Place the patient supine with the head flexed on the chest
Perform head tilt and chin lift (or jaw thrust) and apply high-flow oxygen
Proceed directly to tracheal intubation without further assessment

questions.correctOptionText: Perform head tilt and chin lift (or jaw thrust) and apply high-flow oxygen

distractorRationale.a: Sedation would deepen the loss of airway tone.
distractorRationale.b: Flexion worsens obstruction; the airway opens with extension or jaw thrust.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: simple manoeuvres plus oxygen relieve tongue-based obstruction and buy time.
distractorRationale.d: Intubation is an escalation, used if simple measures fail.

questions.explanation: Snoring with see-saw respiration signals upper airway obstruction, most often from the tongue falling back. Head tilt and chin lift or jaw thrust with high-flow oxygen is the first, least invasive step, and adjuncts or intubation are used only if it fails.

questions.stem: What is the usual method to choose the size of an oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway for an adult?

options.text: Measure from the incisors (centre of the lips) to the angle of the mandible
Always use the largest size available
Choose by the patient's age in decades
Measure from the nose tip to the sternal notch

questions.correctOptionText: Measure from the incisors (centre of the lips) to the angle of the mandible

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the airway should span the distance from the incisors to the angle of the jaw.
distractorRationale.b: An oversized airway can obstruct the larynx or cause trauma.
distractorRationale.c: Age is not used; anatomy is measured.
distractorRationale.d: This is not the standard measure for an OPA.

questions.explanation: The flange rests at the lips while the tip lies near the angle of the mandible, so that the airway holds the tongue clear of the posterior pharynx. Too short fails to lift the tongue, and too long can press the epiglottis down and worsen obstruction.

questions.stem: After intubation the anaesthetist hears equivocal breath sounds and the chest moves poorly. Which finding best confirms tracheal tube placement?

options.text: Misting of the tube during expiration
A rise in heart rate after the tube is passed
A sustained waveform capnography trace with each breath
Absence of gurgling over the epigastrium

questions.correctOptionText: A sustained waveform capnography trace with each breath

distractorRationale.a: Misting is unreliable and can occur with oesophageal intubation.
distractorRationale.b: Heart rate is not specific to tube position.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: a sustained end-tidal CO2 waveform is the reference standard for confirmation.
distractorRationale.d: Auscultation alone gives false reassurance and false alarms.

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is exhaled only from the lungs, so a persistent waveform over several breaths indicates tracheal placement. A flat trace should be treated as oesophageal intubation until proved otherwise, and the tube position re-checked, rather than explained away.

questions.stem: At direct laryngoscopy only the epiglottis can be seen and no part of the glottis. Which Cormack and Lehane grade is this?

options.text: Grade 3
Grade 4
Grade 2
Grade 1

distractorRationale.b: Grade 4 shows neither glottis nor epiglottis.
distractorRationale.c: Grade 2 shows the posterior glottis or arytenoids.
distractorRationale.d: Grade 1 shows most of the glottis.

questions.explanation: The grades describe the best view of the larynx: 1 almost all of the glottis, 2 the posterior glottis, 3 the epiglottis only, 4 no laryngeal structure including the epiglottis. Grades 3 and 4 predict difficult intubation, so a bougie or video laryngoscope is considered early.

questions.stem: During a general anaesthetic, intubation fails after repeated attempts. Facemask ventilation is possible with an oral airway and oxygen saturation is stable. According to DAS-style guidance, which step should follow?

options.text: Proceed straight to a surgical front-of-neck airway
Maintain oxygenation with a supraglottic airway device (Plan B) and involve senior help
Give a second sedative and wait for the saturation to fall
Continue laryngoscopy until successful

questions.correctOptionText: Maintain oxygenation with a supraglottic airway device (Plan B) and involve senior help

distractorRationale.a: Front-of-neck access is for CICO only.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: after failed intubation within the attempt limit, use a supraglottic airway device to maintain oxygenation.
distractorRationale.c: Sedatives would not secure the airway and delay worsens the situation.
distractorRationale.d: Persisting beyond the attempt limit risks trauma and swelling.

questions.explanation: The aim after failed intubation is oxygenation, not intubation at all costs. Plan B is a supraglottic airway device, followed by a decision with the senior anaesthetist (wake the patient, proceed with the device, or secure the airway by another route), always checking current local guidance.

questions.stem: A Guedel (oropharyngeal) airway is well tolerated in a drowsy patient who still has an intact gag reflex.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: An oropharyngeal airway stimulates the base of the tongue and pharynx, so a patient with a gag reflex is likely to gag, vomit or develop laryngospasm. A nasopharyngeal airway is the usual adjunct in a patient who still has airway reflexes.

questions.stem: A transport cylinder of internal volume 5.0 L has a gauge pressure of 90 bar. Assume ideal gas behaviour at constant temperature and treat the usable gas as internal volume multiplied by gauge pressure. The patient receives oxygen at 12 L/min. How long, in minutes, until the cylinder is empty?
questions.explanation: Usable volume is 5.0 L x 90 bar = 450 L at atmospheric pressure. Dividing by the flow of 12 L/min gives 37.5 minutes, so about 37.5 minutes of oxygen in theory; in practice a safety reserve must be kept (check local policy).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is anaesthetised for an elective hernia repair. Three attempts at laryngoscopy fail (grade 3 view), facemask ventilation is difficult, and a supraglottic airway device then fails to produce adequate ventilation. SpO2 is 82% and falling. Explain what is happening and what should be done.
markingGuide: Recognises a 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' (CICO) emergency
Calls for help and declares CICO to the team
Ensures neuromuscular blockade is complete and 100% oxygen is given
Proceeds without delay to emergency front-of-neck access (scalpel-bougie-tube technique)
Avoids further repeated laryngoscopy or device attempts
States that the aim is oxygenation, not intubation
questions.explanation: Failure of Plans A, B and C in a falling-saturation patient defines CICO. Hesitation is the commonest cause of harm, so help is called at once and front-of-neck access is performed; see current DAS guidance.

questions.stem: Explain the principles of preparing for tracheal intubation, and list bedside features that may predict difficulty.
markingGuide: Equipment check: suction, laryngoscope with alternative blades, tubes, bougie, supraglottic airway, front-of-neck kit
Monitoring including waveform capnography and IV access
Verbalising Plans A to D and allocating roles
Predictors: reduced mouth opening, short thyromental distance, high Mallampati class, limited neck extension, prominent incisors or receding jaw, previous difficulty
States that no single test is sensitive enough, and that capnography confirms placement
questions.explanation: Thorough preparation shortens the time to rescue and a plan spoken aloud lets the team act together. Prediction is imperfect, so every anaesthetic is prepared for failure.

questions.stem: Compare oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways, giving the indication, sizing and cautions of each.
markingGuide: OPA: for deeply unconscious patients without a gag reflex
OPA sizing: incisors to angle of the mandible
OPA risks: gagging, vomiting, laryngospasm, obstruction if the wrong size
NPA: tolerated by patients with a gag reflex
NPA cautions: base-of-skull fracture and coagulopathy (epistaxis); lubricated and passed along the nasal floor
Both are adjuncts used after head tilt chin lift or jaw thrust
questions.explanation: Matching the adjunct to the patient's reflexes and injury pattern prevents complications. Both devices only lift the tongue and do not protect against aspiration.
